meaning: one; a (before a measure word); the whole (一天 'all day')

senses.en: one (counting; read yāo in phone and room numbers)
a / one, before a measure word: 一个人, 一杯茶
the whole, all (before a time word): 一天 'all day'

hv.note: Alone, Vietnamese nhất means 'most/first' (đẹp nhất, thứ nhất); it means 'one' only in compounds (duy nhất). Counting 'one' is một. Chinese 'most' is 最.

examples.en: I'd like a cup of tea.
examples.analysis: 一 + measure word 杯 'cup' + 茶: a number normally needs a measure word before a noun (天 'day' and 年 'year' are exceptions: 一天). 我要… 'I want…' is the everyday way to order. Same order as Vietnamese 'một ly trà'.

examples.en: Are you buying one or two?
examples.analysis: 一个 vs 两个: before a measure word, 'two' is 两, not 二. 还是 'or' offers the two options inside a question, so no 吗 is needed. Typical market talk.
Here 一天 means 'the whole day', not 'one day'. 都 sums it up and 没 negates a past action: 一天都没… = 'not … the entire day'. Compare Vietnamese 'cả ngày chưa ăn cơm'.

related.en: two, before a measure word (两个人)
two when counting or reading digits

vn_note: 一 + measure word + noun has the same order as Vietnamese một + classifier + noun: 一杯茶 = một ly trà, 一本书 = một cuốn sách. Learn each noun's measure word as you would cái or con.
hook: 一 is a single stroke: one line for 'one' (二 has two, 三 three).

meaning: very; often just the link before an adjective (我很好 'I'm fine')

senses.en: very; quite (when stressed)
unstressed default link between subject and adjective: 我很好 'I'm fine'

hv.note: Not a Vietnamese word; only a memory aid. Vietnamese says rất or lắm.

examples.analysis: Chinese adjectives act as verbs, so no 是 is needed: 今天 + 很 + 冷. Unstressed 很 is mostly filler, so this is 'it's cold', not necessarily 'very cold'. Bare 今天冷 sounds like a comparison.
A plain 吗 question drops 很: 你家远吗？ Adding 很 stresses the degree, 'is it really far?', so 很 is not filler here. 你家 'your home' needs no 的. Answer 很远 / 不远, not 是 / 不是.

不是很 + adjective = 'not very / not that': a partial negation, softer than a flat 不忙 'I'm not busy'. This 是 is not the 'to be' that links a subject to an adjective; 不是很 is simply the usual frame for negating 很. Vietnamese softens the same way: 'không bận lắm'.

vn_note: Like Vietnamese, Chinese puts an adjective right after the subject, no 'là': 我很好 = tôi khỏe. Don't put 是 before a plain adjective (我是好 is wrong). The one common 是 + 很 frame is 不是很. Unstressed 很 is weaker than rất.

meaning: to know (a fact); to be aware of

senses.en: to know (a fact, a piece of information)
to learn of, to take note: 知道了 'got it, noted'

hv.note: Not a Vietnamese word, but tri 'to know' is familiar from tri thức (知识, knowledge) and tri kỷ.

examples.analysis: 知道了 = 'now I know': 了 marks the change from not knowing to knowing. It is the stock reply to news or instructions, like Vietnamese 'biết rồi'. Said sharply it can sound impatient.

examples.en: Do you know where he lives?
examples.analysis: 知道 takes a whole question as its object: 他住哪儿 keeps normal order, and 吗 at the end makes the whole sentence a yes/no question. Vietnamese: 'Bạn có biết anh ấy sống ở đâu không?'

examples.en: I don't know his name either.
examples.analysis: 知道 is a state, so it is negated with 不 (不知道), not 没. 也 'also' goes before 不. 他叫什么 'what he is called' is the object; Chinese asks names with 叫什么.

collocations.en: you know what? / did you know?

related.en: to know a person or a place (be acquainted)

vn_note: Vietnamese biết covers three Chinese verbs: 知道 for facts (biết chuyện đó), 认识 for people (biết anh ấy = 认识他), 会 for skills (biết nói tiếng Trung = 会说汉语).
hook: 知 is tri, as in tri thức (知识 'knowledge').

meaning: person; people

senses.en: person; people
after a country or city: a person from there (越南人, 北京人)
someone, anyone (有人, 没人)

measure.note: 三个人; polite for guests: 几位 (wèi)?

hv.note: Alone, nhân is not 'person' (that is người), but it lives in compounds: bệnh nhân (病人, patient), nhân dân, cá nhân (个人).

examples.analysis: Country + 人 = a person from there: 哪国人 'which-country person'. The order is the reverse of Vietnamese 'người nước nào': Chinese puts the describer first and 人 last. Answer: 我是越南人.
人很多 'people are many' is the normal way to say 'crowded'. 这儿 'here' is the topic, then 人 + 很多. Compare Vietnamese 'Ở đây đông người quá'.
没 (short for 没有 'there isn't') + 人 = 'no one'; 人 here means 'anybody'. The question form is 有人吗？ 'Anyone here?', what you call out at a door.

vn_note: Order trap: Vietnamese puts người first (người Việt, người bệnh), Chinese puts 人 last (越南人, 病人), the same order as the Hán-Việt bệnh nhân.
hook: 人 is a pictograph of a standing person seen from the side.

meaning: end particle: 'let's…', a softened request, or a guess ('…right?')

senses.en: suggestion: 我们走吧 'let's go'
softens a request or an offer: 你坐吧 'have a seat'
a guess asking for confirmation: '…, right?'

hv.note: Only the sound; unrelated to Vietnamese ba (three, father).

examples.analysis: 我们 + verb + 吧 = 'let's…'. Without 吧, 我们走 is a flat statement ('we're leaving'). Vietnamese uses the same end slot: 'Mình đi thôi' / 'đi nhé'.
吧 turns a statement into a guess: the speaker already thinks so and wants a nod. With 吗 (你是阿梅吗？) it would be a neutral question. Close to Vietnamese 'Chị là Mai đúng không?'

examples.en: You go ahead and eat, I'll be right there.
examples.analysis: 吧 softens an instruction into a friendly suggestion; 你们先吃 alone sounds more abrupt. 先 'first' + verb = 'go ahead and…'. Vietnamese: 'Mọi người cứ ăn trước đi'.

vn_note: 吧 does the job of Vietnamese end words nhé, đi, thôi (đi thôi = 走吧), and in questions of 'chắc… nhỉ?'. 好吧 can sound reluctant, like 'thôi được'.
hook: 口 'mouth' marks a spoken particle; 巴 (bā) gives the sound.

meaning: that; those (farther from the speaker)

senses.en: that (thing, person, situation): 那是什么？
that…, before a measure word + noun: 那个人 'that person'

hv.note: Only the sound; Vietnamese says đó, kia or ấy.

examples.analysis: 那 stands alone as the subject: 那 + 是 + 什么. 什么 stays where the answer goes (那是茶), unlike English 'what' at the front. Vietnamese works the same: 'Đó là cái gì?'

那 + measure word 个 + noun 菜: before most nouns 那 needs a measure word (a few, like 天 in 那天 'that day', take it directly). In speech 那个 is often said nèige. Vietnamese puts đó after the noun (món đó); Chinese puts 那个 before it.

examples.en: I don't want that one, I want this one.
examples.analysis: 那个 alone = 'that one' when the thing is obvious, as when pointing in a shop. 不要那个 vs 要这个 sets 那 against 这 'this'. The subject 我 is not repeated in the second half.

related.en: which? (same shape plus 口, third tone)

vn_note: Order trap: Chinese puts 那 + measure word before the noun (那个人), Vietnamese puts đó after (người đó). At the start of a reply, 那… means 'vậy thì', a separate entry.
hook: 哪 (nǎ, 'which?') is 那 with 口 'mouth' added: the mouth version asks the question.

meaning: to come (toward the speaker); to do or take (standing in for another verb)

senses.en: to come (toward the speaker or the place talked about)
to do, handle, take (replaces a verb): 我来 'let me', 来一个 'one, please'

hv.note: Lai alone is not 'come' in Vietnamese, but it is in tương lai (将来, 'the time to come') and vãng lai (往来, coming and going).

examples.analysis: Time questions go before the verb: 你 + 什么时候 + 来, not 'come when'. Vietnamese does the same for the future: 'Bao giờ bạn đến?'. 来 means 'come to where I am'.

examples.en: He's not coming today after all.
examples.analysis: 不来 = won't come (a plan or a choice). The final 了 marks a change: he was coming, now he isn't. Without 了, 他今天不来 just states that he won't come.
我来 = 'let me (do it)': 来 replaces whatever verb fits (pour the tea, carry the bag, pay). 坐着 'stay sitting'. A common polite offer, like Vietnamese 'Để tôi'.

vn_note: Trap: Vietnamese đến has no direction (tôi đến trường), but 来 means moving toward the speaker or listener. Said from home, 'tôi đến trường' is 我去学校, not 我来学校. 我来 'let me do it' = 'để tôi'.

meaning: all; both (sums up the people or things before it); already

senses.en: all, both: sums up a plural subject (我们都…)
都 + 不/没: none, not any, not a single (他们都不去 'none of them is going', 一个都没有); 不都 is different: 'not all'
already (都…了): 都十点了

hv.note: Đô (thủ đô, đô thị) belongs to this character's other reading, dū 'capital'. For 'all' Vietnamese says đều.

examples.analysis: 都 sits after the plural subject 我们 and before the verb 是; it looks back at who is included. Same slot as Vietnamese đều: 'Chúng tôi đều là người Việt'.
都 + time + 了 = 'it's already…', with a sense of 'that late!'. 快 + verb pushes someone to hurry: 快起床 'get up, quick'.

examples.zh: 这儿我一个人都不认识。
examples.en: I don't know a single person here.
examples.analysis: 一个人 + 都 + 不 = 'not even one person': 都 makes the negative total. 这儿 'here' comes first as the topic. Vietnamese: 'Ở đây tôi không quen ai cả'.

collocations.en: all are; (都是你) it's all your fault

vn_note: 都 sits where Vietnamese đều does: after the subject, before the verb (chúng tôi đều đi = 我们都去). For 'all', don't put it before the subject like English 'all of us'; sentence-initial 都十点了 is the 'already' use.

meaning: general measure word for people and things (一个人, 两个包子)

senses.en: the all-purpose measure word between a number (or 这/那/几) and a noun
这个 / 那个 alone: 'this one / that one'

hv.note: The cá of cá nhân (个人, individual), not cá 'fish'. As a measure word it plays the role of cái, con, người.

examples.analysis: Number + 个 + noun: 两个包子. Before a measure word, 'two' is 两, not 二. Vietnamese has the same slot: 'hai cái bánh bao'.

examples.en: How many kids do you have?
examples.analysis: 几 'how many' also needs the measure word: 几 + 个 + 孩子. Use 几 when you expect a small number (under ten), 多少 for bigger ones.
这 + 个 = 'this one', with the noun dropped because you are pointing at it. 多少钱 'how much money' follows directly, no verb needed. The key shopping question.

vn_note: 个 fills the slot of Vietnamese cái, con, người, đứa: 两个孩子 = hai đứa con. Chinese nouns need a measure word after a number even where Vietnamese has none (ba sinh viên = 三个大学生); time words like 一天, 两年 take none.
hook: Hán-Việt cá, as in cá nhân (个人): 个 counts individual things.

meaning: can; to be able to (because conditions allow); may

senses.en: can, be able to (ability, health, time, conditions)
may, be allowed to (asking permission): 我能…吗？

hv.note: Năng alone in Vietnamese means 'often' (năng về thăm nhà), not 'can'; the 'able' sense lives in năng lực (能力) and khả năng (可能). Say có thể or …được.

examples.analysis: 不能 + verb = 'can't' because of circumstances (busy, sick), not lack of skill. The time word 明天 sits before 不能. Vietnamese: 'Mai tôi không đến được'.
能 + verb + 吗 asks permission politely. 坐这儿 'sit here' is spoken shorthand for 坐在这儿 (posture and placement verbs such as 坐, 站, 住, 放 often drop 在). A typical yes is 可以 or just 坐吧.

examples.en: He's recovered and can go back to work.
examples.analysis: 能 here is regained ability: 病好了 'the illness got better', so now 能上班了 'can go to work again'. Both 了 mark a new situation. Vietnamese: 'Anh ấy khỏi bệnh rồi, đi làm được rồi'.

related.en: can (a learned skill): 会说汉语

vn_note: Vietnamese biết vs có thể maps onto 会 vs 能: biết nói tiếng Trung = 会说汉语 (a skill), không đến được = 不能来 (circumstances).
hook: Hán-Việt năng, as in năng lực (能力, ability).

meaning: to go (to a place); to go and do something

senses.en: to go to a place: 去 + place (去医院)
to go and do something: 去 + verb (去吃饭)

hv.note: Not a word on its own in Vietnamese; it lives in vé khứ hồi (a round trip; Chinese says 来回/往返) and quá khứ (过去, the past).

examples.analysis: 去 + place, where the place is the question word 哪儿 'where'. It stays in the object slot instead of moving to the front as in English, exactly like Vietnamese 'Bạn đi đâu?'. Also a casual hello between people who know each other.

examples.zh: 我去商店买东西，你要什么？
examples.en: I'm going to the shop to pick up a few things. What do you want?
examples.analysis: 去 + place + verb: the place (商店) comes right after 去 and the purpose (买东西) follows, in the order things happen. No word for 'to' or 'in order to' is needed; Vietnamese works the same way: 'Tôi đi cửa hàng mua đồ'.

examples.en: I'm too tired today; I'm not going after all.
examples.analysis: 去 with no object: both people know where. 不去 = won't go, and the final 了 marks a change of plan ('not going anymore'), like Vietnamese 'thôi, tôi không đi nữa'.

related.en: to walk; to leave (我走了 'I'm off')
to arrive; 去 is setting off, 到 is getting there

vn_note: 去 is 'đi' only as 'go to a place / go and do'. When 'đi' means 'walk' or 'leave', Chinese uses 走: 走路 = đi bộ, 我走了 = tôi đi đây.
hook: Hán-Việt khứ, as in vé khứ hồi (a round trip): khứ = go, hồi = come back.

meaning: not (for things that did not happen); not have (short for 没有)

senses.en: did not; have not (yet): denies that an action happened (没去)
to not have; there is no (= 没有): 没钱, 没电

hv.note: Not the native Vietnamese 'một' (one). Hán-Việt 没 only shows up in words like mai một (埋没, to fade away, be lost).

examples.analysis: Verb use: 没 = 没有 'not have', so 没电 is literally 'has no power'. The final 了 says this is a new situation (it just ran out), like Vietnamese 'điện thoại hết pin rồi'.

examples.en: I didn't go yesterday; I was too busy.
examples.analysis: Adverb use: 没 + verb denies that something happened. For 'did not do', use 没, not 不: 我昨天不去 does not mean 'I didn't go yesterday'. (不 still appears in past-time sentences about wishes and states, e.g. 昨天我不想去.) No 了 is added: 没 alone already says it didn't happen.

examples.en: You didn't go to work today?
examples.analysis: 没 + verb + 吗 asks a yes/no question about something that did not happen. With a negative like this it often shows mild surprise, like Vietnamese 'Hôm nay bạn không đi làm à?'. The short answer 'no, I didn't' is 没有; 'yes, I did' is 上了.

related.en: not: for the present, future, habits and wishes
full form of 没; also used alone as 'no, I didn't'

vn_note: 没 covers 'chưa', past 'không' and 'không có': 我没吃 = tôi chưa ăn, 我昨天没去 = hôm qua tôi không đi, 没钱 = không có tiền. 'Không' for habits or refusals is 不: 我不吃肉 = tôi không ăn thịt.
hook: 氵 (water) on the left: the original sense was 'to sink under water', still read mò in that sense.

meaning: and (between nouns); with, together with (a person)

senses.en: and: joins two nouns or pronouns (茶和包子)
with; together with: 和 + person + verb (和他说话)

hv.note: Vietnamese hoà means peace, a draw or to mix (hoà bình 和平, hoà nhau, hoà tan); it never means 'and', which is và / với.

examples.zh: 我要一杯茶和一个包子。
examples.en: I'll have a tea and a steamed bun.
examples.analysis: Conjunction: 和 links two noun phrases, 一杯茶 and 一个包子, just like 'và' in 'một ly trà và một cái bánh bao'. It joins things, not whole sentences.
Preposition: 和 + person + 一起 + verb = do something together with someone. The 和 phrase sits BEFORE the verb, while Vietnamese puts it after ('Bạn đi với ai?'). The question word 谁 stays in place.

examples.en: I'm not talking to him anymore.
examples.analysis: 和 + person + 说话 = talk with someone. The negative 不 normally goes before the whole 和 phrase, not between it and the verb. The final 了 means 'anymore', a change of attitude, like 'tôi không nói chuyện với nó nữa'.

related.en: with; and: more colloquial, very common in the north
and also: adds an afterthought or a whole new sentence, which 和 cannot do

vn_note: 'Và' can link two actions or two sentences; 和 mostly links nouns and pronouns (formal writing also joins set pairs like 学习和工作), never whole sentences. For another action or sentence, use a comma, 也, or 还有.
hook: 禾 (grain) + 口 (mouth); 禾 is also read hé and gives the sound.

meaning: they; them (a mixed or all-male group of people)

senses.en: they; them: a group of people, mixed or male (the same form as subject and object)

hv.note: Not a Vietnamese word. Tha (他, other) appears in tha hương (他乡, a place far from home) and vị tha (living for others).

examples.analysis: 他们 as subject: 他们 + 是 + noun. The verb never changes for plural, and 同学 needs no plural ending either: Chinese nouns normally do not mark number, so 我的同学 can mean 'my classmate' or 'my classmates', and 他们 tells you it is several.
他们 + 去 + 哪儿 + 了: the final 了 says they have already left, so this asks where they went, not where they are going. Same shape as Vietnamese 'Họ đi đâu rồi?'.
他们 as object, after the verb, with no change of form: 'they' and 'them' are one word, just like Vietnamese 'họ'. 不认识 = not know (a person), not be acquainted with, as in 'tôi không quen họ'.

related.en: they: an all-female group; same sound

vn_note: 他们 = 'họ / bọn họ'. 们 is like 'các' in 'các bạn' (你们), but it goes on people (and personified animals), not on ordinary things: 'các cuốn sách' cannot be 书们.
hook: Both characters have 亻 (person). 们 = 亻 + 门 (mén), which gives the sound.

meaning: to arrive; to reach; until (a time)

senses.en: to arrive; to get to (a place): 到家, 到了
until; up to (a time or point): 工作到十点
after a verb: reached, managed to (看到, 找到)

hv.note: Not used alone; đáo survives in đáo hạn (a loan reaching its due date; Chinese says 到期) and chu đáo (周到, thorough). Everyday Vietnamese says đến / tới.

examples.analysis: 到 alone, no place needed: both sides know where. 马上 'right away' goes before the verb, and the plain verb covers the near future, the way Vietnamese says 'Tôi tới liền!'.
到 + place + 了 = has arrived. Friends text this after an evening out to check you got home safely. 到家 needs no word for 'at' or 'to': the arrival is inside 到.

还没 + 到 = not here yet (vẫn chưa tới). Arriving is an event that has not happened, so 'hasn't arrived' is 没到, not 不到 (不到 usually means 'less than / not yet', as in 不到十点 'not yet ten o'clock'). 车 here is a car, bus or taxi, whichever vehicle you are waiting for.

collocations.en: to see; to catch sight of

related.en: to go; 去 is the trip, 到 the arrival

vn_note: 到 matches 'đến / tới' closely: arrive (đến nơi), until (làm đến mười giờ = 工作到十点). Trap: 'đến' meaning 'come' is 来: 你来吗？ = bạn có đến không?
hook: 至 (to arrive) + 刂, a knife (刀 dāo) that only gives the sound.

meaning: right; correct; (as a reply) yes, that's right

senses.en: right; correct (你说的对)
yes, right: as a one-word answer (对！) or tag (对不对？)

hv.note: Vietnamese đối means facing, opposing or towards (đối diện, phản đối 反对, đối với); it never means 'correct', which is đúng.

examples.analysis: 对 as a one-word 'yes': it confirms what the other person guessed (你是医生吗？). Chinese has no all-purpose 'yes'; 对 is the go-to reply when the guess is correct, like 'đúng rồi'.

你说的 = 'what you said', and 对 is the predicate: 'what you said is right'. No 是 is needed before an adjective. Books usually write this 你说得对 (with 得); 你说的对 is the common casual form. Vietnamese: 'bạn nói đúng'.
对不对 ('right or not?') added at the end turns a statement into a check question, like Vietnamese '…, đúng không?'. Answer 对 for yes, 不对 for no.

related.en: 'yes, it is': confirms identity; 对 confirms a guess is correct

vn_note: 对 = 'đúng'. As a reply 对 ≈ 'đúng rồi', and 对不对？ ≈ 'đúng không?'. The 'towards' use (对他好, tốt với anh ấy) is 对's other entry.

meaning: also; too; (with a negative) not … either

senses.en: also; too: placed before the verb (我也去)
not … either: 也 + 不 / 没 (我也不知道)

hv.note: No everyday Vietnamese word; it survives only in the idiom chi hồ giả dã (之乎者也, pedantic bookish talk). The dã of dã ngoại, hoang dã is 野 (wild).

examples.analysis: The everyday 'me too': 也 + 是, literally 'I also am (so)'. 也 goes before a verb or adjective, so the full reply is 我也是. In quick casual replies people do clip it to just 我也 ('me too!'), but as a beginner say 我也是.
也 sits after the subject and before the verb, never at the end like English 'too'. Same slot as 'cũng' in 'Bạn cũng đi à?'. 吗 makes it a yes/no question.
也 + 不 = 'also not', i.e. 'not … either'. 也 comes first, then the negative. English switches to 'either'; Chinese keeps 也, as Vietnamese keeps 'cũng': tôi cũng không biết.

related.en: all; both: 也 comes first (我们也都去)
also; in addition (还有, 还要)

vn_note: 也 = 'cũng', in the same position: subject + 也 + verb, so 我也很忙 = tôi cũng bận. Like 'cũng', it never goes before the subject: 也我去 is wrong.

meaning: still; (not) yet; also, else, in addition

senses.en: still: something continues (还在…, 还没…)
also; else; in addition (还要, 还有)
fairly; passably (还好 'not bad')

hv.note: Vietnamese hoàn (hoàn trả, hoàn tiền) is 'give back', which is 还 read huán, a separate entry. The 'still' sense has no Vietnamese cognate.

examples.analysis: 还 + 在 + verb = still in the middle of doing it. 还 sits right before the verb phrase, like 'vẫn' in 'Bạn vẫn đang làm à?'. A classic evening text from family.
还没 + verb = not yet (vẫn chưa). Plain 我没吃饭 can already mean 'I haven't eaten' (tôi chưa ăn); 还 adds 'still', stressing that it hasn't happened so far but is expected to.
What a shop or restaurant clerk asks. 还 + 要 = 'want in addition', and 别的 = 'something else'. The subject 你 is dropped. Vietnamese: 'Còn lấy gì nữa không?'

vn_note: 还 lines up with 'còn / vẫn': 还在 = vẫn còn (đang), 还没 = vẫn chưa, 还要 = còn muốn (thêm), 还有 = còn có. Read huán it means 'trả lại', another entry.
hook: 辶 (walking) points to the original meaning, 'to go back' (huán, Hán-Việt hoàn).

meaning: to give; for, to (someone), before a verb

senses.en: to give: 给 + person + thing (给我一杯水)
for; to (someone): 给 + person + verb (给你打电话)

hv.note: Vietnamese cấp keeps 'give', but only officially: cấp giấy phép, cấp học bổng, cung cấp (供给 gōngjǐ, where 给 is read jǐ). Spoken 给 is the plain 'cho / đưa'.

examples.analysis: Verb with two objects: 给 + person (我) + thing (一杯水). The person comes first, as in Vietnamese 'cho tôi một ly nước'. 请 at the front makes it polite.
Preposition: 给 + person comes BEFORE the verb 打电话. Vietnamese puts it after ('gọi điện cho bạn'), so the order flips. The time word 晚上 goes before 给.

examples.en: Did you give him the money?
examples.analysis: The same 给 + person + thing pattern, as a question. 了 marks the giving as done, and 吗 asks yes or no. Answer 给了 (yes) or 没给 (no).

related.en: to give as a present; to see someone off

vn_note: 给 does both jobs of 'cho': give (给我 = cho tôi) and 'for / to'. Trap: Vietnamese puts 'cho + person' after the verb, Chinese usually puts 给 + person before it: 'gọi cho bạn' = 给你打电话.
hook: Hán-Việt cấp, as in cung cấp (供给 gōngjǐ, to supply); in that word 给 is read jǐ.

meaning: to do; to make; to cook

senses.en: to do (a job, a task): 做什么
to make; to cook (做饭, 做菜)

hv.note: No Vietnamese word. The tố of tố cáo is a different character (诉, to accuse).

examples.en: What do you do for work?
examples.analysis: 做 + 什么 + 工作 = 'do what job'. The question word 什么 sits where the answer would go, as in Vietnamese 'Bạn làm nghề gì?'. A typical answer: 我是医生.
做 = cook here. 晚饭 'dinner' is put first as the topic, then 我来做 = 'I'll do it': 我来 + verb is the usual way to volunteer for a job ('let me …'). 吧 softens it into an offer.

examples.en: I don't know how to do this.
examples.analysis: 不会 + 做 = can't do it (don't have the skill). 这个 'this' (a task, a form, a dish) is put first as the topic. Vietnamese does the same: 'Cái này tôi không biết làm'.

vn_note: 做 = 'làm' in most uses: 做什么 = làm gì. It also covers 'nấu': 做饭 = nấu cơm. But having a job ('làm ở…') is 工作: 我在医院工作 = tôi làm ở bệnh viện.
